title: Eḍ-ḍiyaafe — visiting, and the road ahead
goal: Visit and host with the right etiquette — the heart of Levantine culture — then see how what you've learned connects to Standard Arabic and other dialects.
bekal: get through a whole visit, from the door to saying goodbye
answer blessings and compliments with the right reply
see the bridges from Levantine to Standard Arabic and the neighboring dialects

dialogs.title: حَكِي — عَ الْعَشَا بِبَيْت لَيْلَى
dialogs.intro: Friday evening. Budi arrives at Laila's family home with a box of sweets and is welcomed by her mother, Umm Rami.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.baca: ahlan w sahlan! tfaḍḍal, nawwart el-bēt.
lines.id: Welcome! Come in, you light up the house.
lines.literal: family and ease! go-ahead, you-lit the-house.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: It's you who lights it up. Here are some sweets.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: Oh, you shouldn't have! There was no need.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: Please, come into the living room. What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أَيّ شِي، مَا فِي دَاعِي تِتْعَبِي.
lines.baca: ayy shi, ma fi daa‘i tit‘abi.
lines.id: Anything, don't go to any trouble.
lines.literal: which thing, not there-is reason you-tire.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: What trouble! I'll bring you some coffee.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: Please come to the table. Enjoy.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: وَاللَّه شِي بْيِفْتَح النَّفْس! تِسْلَم إِيدِك.
lines.baca: walla shi byiftah en-nafs! tislam iidik.
lines.id: Wow, that looks delicious! Your cooking is wonderful.
lines.literal: by-God thing it-opens the-appetite! may-they-be-safe hands-your.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.text: صَحْتَين. كُول كَمَان، مَا أَكَلِت شِي!
lines.baca: sahtēn. kuul kamaan, ma akalt shi!
lines.id: Enjoy. Have some more, you haven't eaten a thing!
lines.literal: two-healths. eat also, not you-ate thing!

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: May your table always be full.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: دَايْمًا. صَار لَازِم رَوِّح، اَلْوَقْت تْأَخَّر.
lines.baca: daayman. ṣaar laazim rawwih, el-wa’t t’akhkhar.
lines.id: Always. I have to go home, it's late.
lines.literal: always. became must I-go-home, the-time late.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.text: بَكِّير! بَسّ مَاشِي. تِكْرَم، وْبِتْشَرَّفْنَا دَايْمًا.
lines.baca: bakkiir! bass maashi. tikram, w bitsharrafna daayman.
lines.id: It's early! But all right. Go in peace, and you're always welcome here.
lines.literal: early! but walking. honored, and you-honor-us always.

notes: **The phrase نَوَّرِت is the warmest welcome there is.** Literally "you lit up (this house)," it has a must-say reply: اَلنُّور نُورَك ("the light is yours"). To a woman: اَلنُّور نُورِك. Learn the pair by heart — you'll hear it in every home you enter.

**⚠️ Refusing a guest's gift and refusing second helpings are an expected exchange, not real refusals.** The host says مَا كَان لَازِم; the guest brings it anyway. The host says كُول كَمَان; the guest declines once, the host insists, and the guest accepts a little. Skipping the dance — accepting or refusing straight away — feels awkward either way.

**The phrase شُو هَالتَّعَب! literally means "what is this trouble!"** and means "you shouldn't have." The reply is وَلَا شِي ("it's nothing"). The pattern هَال… (from هَاد + اَل) points to something right in front of you, and you'll hear it a lot.
**You met سُفْرَة دَايْمِة in unit 12** as the reply to praise for the food. Here it appears in its natural setting: the host says it at the end of the meal, and the guest replies دَايْمًا.

**Leaving a Levantine home takes three or four rounds.** The host will say بَكِّير! ("it's early!") at least twice, and it isn't empty talk — they really want you to stay longer. Standing up, saying thank you, then sitting down for another five minutes is perfectly normal.

**The phrase بِتْشَرَّفْنَا دَايْمًا means "you're always welcome here."** It's the most polite way to end a visit, and the reply is اَلشَّرَف إِلِي ("the honor is mine"). With that, the whole circle of visiting etiquette is neatly closed.

grammars.title: Blessings and replies — learn them in pairs
body: Levantine Arabic is full of paired blessings, and not answering one feels like ignoring an outstretched hand. Here are the ones you'll hear most.
after: If you really can't remember the reply, one sentence fits almost all of them: **اَللَّه يْخَلِّيك** *alla ykhalliik* ("God keep you"). It's polite, warm, and never out of place.
Notice that all these blessings take the possessive endings you learned in unit 4. To a woman, change ـَك to ـِك — for example اَللَّه يْخَلِّيكِ، سَلَامْتِك، تِسْلَم إِيدِك.

grammars.title: From Levantine to Standard Arabic and the neighbors
body: Everything you've learned in this book isn't an island. This table shows how close it is to Standard Arabic and to Egyptian Arabic, which you'll also hear a lot.
after: What to take from this table: **the sentence frame is the same; only a handful of short, frequent words differ.** If you move on to Standard Arabic or Egyptian, you don't need to change how you think — just about thirty words.

The b- prefix on verbs is shared by Levantine and Egyptian, and doesn't exist in Standard Arabic. In reverse, i'raab (the ـُ ـَ ـِ endings) exists in Standard Arabic and in neither dialect. Those are the two big differences; the rest is detail.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Four things to know before entering a Levantine home
items: **Shoes.** Some homes take them off, some don't. Ask اِشْلَح؟ *ishlah?* ("should I take them off?") or look at what's by the door.
**Sit where you're shown.** The host will point you to a seat, usually the best one in the room. Refusing it just makes things awkward.
**Don't over-praise objects.** If you admire something too enthusiastically, your host may feel obliged to give it to you. This really happens.
**Don't arrive exactly on time for social invitations.** Fifteen to thirty minutes after the stated time is what's expected — the host is still getting ready.

sections.title: Congratulations — look what you can do

blocks.text: Twenty units done. Before you close this book, take a moment to see how far you've come — because progress in a language almost never feels like progress from the inside.

items: **You can start a conversation with anyone** — greet, introduce yourself, ask how someone is in three different ways, and handle small talk without thinking.
**You can manage daily life on your own** — rent a room, shop and bargain, order food, take public transport, and go to the pharmacy when you're ill.
**You've mastered the whole A1 verb framework** — the present with b-, ongoing actions with عَم, the future with رَح, the past with endings, and the bare form after بَدِّي، لَازِم، مُمْكِن، فِيني.
**You can tell a story** — about your family, your day, yesterday, and your plans for next week, linked with بَعْدَين، لَمَّا، قَبِل مَا، لَإِنّ.
**You know the etiquette**, which is what learners of Arabic from books most rarely have: when to refuse, when to insist, when to offer a blessing, and how to reply.

blocks.title: Three things to do next week
items: **Watch a Syrian or Lebanese film with Arabic subtitles.** You'll be surprised how much you already catch — and the words you miss will stick, because you already know the sentence shapes.
**Find a native speaker to talk to every week.** Twenty minutes a week beats any book, including this one.
**Reread the unit 1 dialogue today.** It'll feel far easier than the first time you read it, and that's all the proof you need.

blocks.text: And to close this book, a blessing you've earned: يَعْطِيك الْعَافْيِة عَ التَّعَب. *(ya‘ṭiik el-‘aafye ‘a et-ta‘ab — may God give you strength for your hard work.)* You already know the reply — for example اَللَّه يْعَافِيك.
